title: Two friends at the festival
hook: Upatissa and Kolita watch a festival and suddenly find it empty

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poem, closed, and your line: the life, retold. Did you tell someone a piece of the Buddha's life? Today a new block begins: the great disciples, the people who followed him. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

Same seats as last year. Same hill above the city. Same crowd, same plays, same music, same jokes landing in the same places. Two young men from good families sit side by side in the best seats, as they always do at this festival. Other years, they laughed at the funny parts and cried at the sad ones and threw gifts to the performers. This year, the jokes land, and neither of them laughs. The sad scene plays, and neither of them cries. Each one glances over and notices the other has gone quiet too.
screen: `SAME SEATS, SAME HILL.` → `THE JOKES LAND, NOBODY LAUGHS.` → `BOTH OF THEM, QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the two friends. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita. The commentaries say they were sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha, close friends since childhood, each with a circle of young companions around him. Later they'll be known by other names, Sariputta and Moggallana. But not yet. Right now they're two well-off young men at a festival. Second, the silence. The commentary tells it simply. Kolita turns to his friend: you don't seem to be enjoying yourself today. What's wrong? And Upatissa answers with a question of his own: what is there to look at here? Before long, all these people, the actors, the crowd, the two of them, will be gone. And here we sit, laughing. Third, the turn. It turns out Kolita has been thinking the same thing. Neither of them talked the other into it. They arrived at the same emptiness, in the same seats, on the same afternoon. Nothing about the festival was wrong. The plays weren't worse. The music wasn't worse. What had changed was them. Fourth, the question that's left. They don't stay sad, and they don't go home and pretend. They decide, together, that they need to look for a way out of birth and death, a release that the festival can't give. And that's the end of today's story. Notice how close it sits to the prince's own. He saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and the palace music went flat. These two never leave their seats. The emptiness finds them in the middle of the fun. The show was empty.
screen: `UPATISSA AND KOLITA.` · `WHAT IS THERE TO LOOK AT?` · `BOTH THINKING THE SAME THING.` · `A WAY OUT, NOT A WAY HOME.` · then, large: `THE SHOW WAS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice when fun feels hollow. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a moment, recent or long ago, when something meant to be fun went flat: a party, a show, a scroll through your phone, a holiday you'd waited for. No need to judge it or fix it. Just remember the feeling, honestly. What were you hungry for that the fun couldn't give? Let the question sit without an answer. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Upatissa. One of two friends who sit through the festival they loved and find it suddenly empty, with his friend Kolita feeling the same. Today's word.
Your line: the show was empty. Today, if something meant to be fun goes flat, don't scroll past the feeling. Ask what you were really looking for. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples; in some Theravada temples images of the two stand on either side of the Buddha, and their story is told in sermons and at festivals.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sariputta and Moggallana were always monks.
what it means: they were two well-off young friends who found a festival empty, and went looking for something more.
what a scholar hears: the festival scene comes from the commentaries, such as the Dhammapada commentary; the Vinaya begins their story with them already wanderers (Mahavagga 1).

sources.ref: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada Atthakatha) on verses 11–12, the story of Sariputta and Moggallana

notes: All material paraphrased (Burlingame's Buddhist Legends, 1921, is not on the validator list).

Confirm the festival details in the Dhammapada commentary (and the parallel in the Anguttara/Theragatha commentaries): the hilltop festival at Rajagaha (Giragga), their laughing, weeping and giving gifts in earlier years, this year's silence, Kolita's question, Upatissa's answer. The commentary's answer includes a span of years ('within a hundred years'); the script says 'before long' to avoid a number.
'Close friends since childhood' and 'sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha' follow the commentary; tradition also says they were born on the same day (not used).
Comparison with the prince's sights is internal to the tradition (no other path compared).
howItsDone: the two chief disciples flanking the Buddha in Theravada temples; confirm.
Editor: Sariputta and Moggallana are the names the discourses use, so 'later tradition knows them' became 'later they'll be known'; howItsDone 'often' softened to 'in some'.

Audit: 'these two don't need a road trip' (a quip about the prince's chariot rides) made 'these two never leave their seats'; unclear 'neither of them dragged the other there' made 'talked the other into it'.
